subject: paediatrics
title: Microdeletion Syndromes: DiGeorge, Williams and Cri-du-Chat

steps.tx: Submicroscopic chromosomal microdeletions spanning contiguous gene clusters escape standard light microscopic detection. The most prevalent microdeletion syndrome is **DiGeorge 22q11 deletion**, also designated as velocardiofacial syndrome, occurring in approximately one in four thousand live births. It is caused by a heterozygous microdeletion of roughly three megabases at band 22q11.2, usually arising de novo due to non-allelic homologous recombination between low-copy repeats.
steps.say: DiGeorge syndrome is the most common microdeletion syndrome, affecting one in four thousand births. A three-megabase deletion on chromosome 22q11.2 disrupts embryonic pharyngeal arch development.

rows: Severely depressed serum calcium and PTH
Hypoplasia or aplasia of thymus gland
Absent thymic shadow on chest radiograph
Interrupted aortic arch type B, truncus

steps.tx: Defective neural crest cell migration into the branchial apparatus disrupts multiple organ systems. The diverse clinical manifestations are summarized by the **CATCH-22 acronym**: Cardiac conotruncal defects, Abnormal facies, Thymic hypoplasia, Cleft palate or velopharyngeal insufficiency, and Hypocalcaemia secondary to parathyroid hypoplasia. Neonates frequently present during the first week of life with hypocalcaemic tetany, cyanotic heart disease, or nasal regurgitation of feeds.
steps.say: The CATCH-22 acronym summarizes cardiac defects, abnormal facies, thymic hypoplasia, cleft palate, and hypocalcaemia. Newborns often present with hypocalcaemic seizures and cyanotic heart lesions.

left.title: Cardiac Anomalies in 22q11
points: Interrupted aortic arch type B (pathognomonic)
Persistent truncus arteriosus
Tetralogy of Fallot (conotruncal defect)
Aberrant right subclavian artery

right.title: Immunological and Endocrine Deficits
points: Parathyroid hypoplasia causing severe hypocalcaemia
Thymic aplasia producing CD3+ T-cell lymphopenia
Susceptibility to viral and fungal pathogens
Irradiated blood products required for transfusions

steps.tx: Parathyroid hypoplasia provokes sudden life-threatening neuromuscular excitability in the first days of life. Severe neonatal **hypocalcaemia in DiGeorge** manifests as jitteriness, carpopedal spasm, stridor, prolonged QT intervals on electrocardiograms, and intractable seizures resistant to standard anticonvulsants. Emergency management requires intravenous calcium gluconate under cardiac monitoring, followed by oral calcium supplements and active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol) to maintain euglycaemic neuromuscular stability.
steps.say: Parathyroid hypoplasia produces neonatal hypocalcaemic seizures and carpopedal spasm. Treat immediately with intravenous calcium gluconate followed by daily oral calcitriol and calcium.

rows: Prostaglandin E1 to keep ductus open

steps.tx: Microdeletions encompassing the elastin locus on chromosome 7 produce distinctive vascular and behavioural phenotypes. The contiguous gene syndrome **Williams-Beuren syndrome** is caused by a 7q11.23 microdeletion involving the ELN (elastin) gene. Affected children exhibit classic elfin facies with broad foreheads, flattened nasal bridges, full cheeks, stellate iris patterns, supravalvular aortic stenosis, infantile hypercalcaemia, and a cocktail party personality featuring extreme empathy and hyper-sociability.
steps.say: Williams syndrome features a 7q11.23 deletion including the elastin gene. Children show elfin facies, supravalvular aortic stenosis, infantile hypercalcaemia, and a hyper-sociable cocktail party personality.

left.title: Williams Syndrome Cardiovascular
points: Supravalvular aortic stenosis (SVAS) in 75%
Peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis
Systemic hypertension from arterial elastopathy
Requires serial echocardiographic surveillance

right.title: Williams Syndrome Neurobehavioural
points: Cocktail party personality with excessive sociability
Affectionate, highly empathetic, fluent verbal skills
Severe visuospatial cognitive impairment
Infantile idiopathic hypercalcaemia in early months

steps.tx: Terminal deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 causes a pathognomonic acoustic phenotype. The congenital disorder **cri du chat syndrome** is caused by partial deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5, specifically band 5p15.2. In early infancy, the child produces a high-pitched, monotone, cat-like mewing cry resulting from abnormal laryngeal development and cerebral hypoplasia, accompanied by severe microcephaly, hypertelorism, round moon facies, and severe intellectual disability.
steps.say: Cri-du-chat syndrome results from a 5p chromosome deletion. The infant produces a characteristic high-pitched cat-like cry due to laryngeal dysgenesis, accompanied by microcephaly and severe mental delay.

steps.tx: Standard G-banded karyotyping lacks optical resolution to detect submicroscopic contiguous gene deletions. The diagnostic technique **fluorescence in situ hybridization** (FISH) utilizes fluorescently labelled DNA probes complementary to specific deleted regions such as 22q11.2 or 7q11.23, demonstrating absent fluorescent hybridization signals on the deleted chromosome. Chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) provides modern genome-wide copy number resolution, detecting submicroscopic gains and losses simultaneously.
steps.say: Fluorescence in situ hybridization and chromosomal microarray detect submicroscopic deletions invisible on routine karyotypes. Probes highlight missing genes on chromosomes 22q and 7q.

left.title: Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization (FISH)
points: Targeted interrogation of suspected specific locus
Rapid turnaround time within 24 to 48 hours
Requires prior clinical hypothesis of deleted region

right.title: Chromosomal Microarray (CMA)
points: Genome-wide scan for copy number variants
Does not require a pre-test clinical hypothesis
Current first-tier diagnostic test for microdeletions

steps.tx: Severe thymic aplasia creates critical risks of graft-versus-host disease during emergency transfusions. Complete absence of mature T-lymphocytes mandates that all blood products must be **irradiated cellular transfusions** to eliminate viable donor lymphocytes, preventing fatal transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease. Live viral vaccines like MMR, rotavirus, and varicella are strictly contraindicated until lymphocyte subset flow cytometry confirms adequate CD3+ and CD4+ T-cell counts.
steps.say: Children with complete DiGeorge thymic aplasia require irradiated blood products to prevent fatal graft-versus-host disease. Live vaccines are contraindicated until T-cell counts are confirmed adequate.

rows: Required for all cellular blood transfusions
CD4+ count >500/uL and normal mitogen response
Initiate in infancy until immune recovery

steps.tx: Comprehensive cardiac and cleft palate repair demands coordinated staged surgical interventions. Infant feeding difficulties from **velopharyngeal incompetence** require specialized cleft feeding bottles to prevent aspiration. Corrective open-heart surgery for conotruncal lesions must be performed under strict calcium stabilization, while early speech pathology and pharyngeal flap procedures improve intelligibility and prevent chronic social isolation.
steps.say: Managing DiGeorge requires cardiac surgery with calcium support, cleft feeding techniques to prevent aspiration, and pharyngeal surgery to correct hypernasal speech.

left.title: Cardiovascular Corrective Surgery
points: Repair interrupted arch or truncus in infancy
Continuous perioperative calcium monitoring
Avoid hypocalcaemic myocardial depression

right.title: Palatal and Airway Rehabilitation
points: Special Haberman feeder for cleft palate
Pharyngeal flap for velopharyngeal insufficiency
Aggressive surveillance for chronic otitis media
